safetyNote: Laccaria amethystina is listed as edible by DGfM and VAPKO, but identify every collection carefully and cook it thoroughly. ANSES documented a collector seeking amethyst deceivers who instead collected poisonous Mycena rosea. This Laccaria can accumulate arsenic, especially on contaminated ground; avoid collecting near former military grounds, mining and industrial sites, and heavily trafficked roads. Have any uncertain specimen checked by a mushroom expert.

sections.title: Amethyst cap that fades
sections.text: The thin cap is usually 2–6 cm across, first convex, then flatter or wavy with a shallow central depression. Fresh, moist fruit bodies can be vividly amethyst violet; ageing or drying changes them towards violet-brown, pale lilac or almost whitish. The surface becomes matt or finely scaly, and the thin margin may be scalloped and somewhat translucent-striate. Colour alone is an unreliable identifier.

sections.title: Thick, distant gills and slender stem
sections.text: The gills are conspicuously thick, widely spaced and irregular, violet when young, sometimes appearing whitish as pale spore dust accumulates. They meet the stem broadly and can run down it a very short distance. The long, slender, often bent stem is violet with whitish lengthwise fibres and a slightly downy basal mycelium. It is tough and fibrous, becoming hollow in mature specimens. There is no ring or volva. The cap flesh is thin and pale violet; the spore print is whitish.

sections.title: Where it grows and what resembles it
sections.text: This fungus grows singly or in groups on leaf litter or among moss in moist woodland, commonly with broadleaf trees but also in conifer woods, from summer into autumn in Europe. Mycena rosea and M. pura can be pink-lilac but have paler gills and a strong radish-like smell; ANSES records a poisoning confusion involving M. rosea. Robust purple blewits such as Lepista nuda and L. sordida also differ in build and gill arrangement. Check the whole fungus, including its gills, rather than relying on the purple cap.

sections.title: Edibility and arsenic precaution
sections.text: DGfM and Swiss VAPKO include the species on edible mushroom lists. The fibrous stem is normally discarded. DGfM advises sufficient cooking and moderate amounts for edible mushrooms, and warns that this species can accumulate arsenic compounds, especially on polluted soils. A peer-reviewed Danish study found much higher arsenic in a specimen from contaminated soil than in samples from uncontaminated beech woods; this is a site-dependent hazard, not a visible identification trait. Do not collect food mushrooms from suspect sites.

traits: Thin 2–6 cm amethyst-violet cap, convex then flat or shallowly depressed, fading strongly on drying
Thick, very widely spaced violet gills, broadly attached and occasionally very shortly decurrent
Slender, bent, tough violet stem with whitish longitudinal fibres; hollow mainly in maturity
No ring or volva; thin pale-violet flesh; whitish spore print
Moist broadleaf and conifer woods, on litter or in moss, summer to autumn
Edible listing, but lookalike and arsenic-contamination precautions are essential
